title: "How the estimates work"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.show = "hold", dpi = 96)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(drawn)
```

This article sets out what `ht_total()` and `ht_mean()` compute, which variance
estimator each design gets and why, and how each one was checked. Everything
here is design-based: the population values are fixed, and the only randomness
is which rows the design selected (Särndal, Swensson and Wretman 1992).

## The estimators

A design gives every frame row $k$ an inclusion probability $\pi_k$ — the
chance it lands in the sample — and every pair of rows a joint probability
$\pi_{kl}$. `inclusion_prob()` and `joint_prob()` compute them from the design
and the frame, before anything is drawn.

**The total** is the Horvitz-Thompson estimator (Horvitz and Thompson 1952):

$$\hat Y = \sum_{k \in s} \frac{y_k}{\pi_k}.$$

It is unbiased for the frame total *provided every row has $\pi_k > 0$*. That
proviso is why `draw()` warns when a stratum is allocated no rows, and why
`sample_summary()` counts unreachable rows.

**The mean** defaults to the Hájek estimator (Hájek 1971), a ratio of two
Horvitz-Thompson totals:

$$\hat{\bar Y} = \frac{\sum_{s} y_k / \pi_k}{\sum_{s} 1 / \pi_k}.$$

Its variance is the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson total of the linearised
residuals $z_k = (y_k - \hat{\bar Y}) / \hat N$ (Deville 1999), so every
variance estimator below serves means as well as totals. A proportion is the
mean of a 0/1 variable.

**Domains** — sites, regions, months — use the whole sample with $y$ set to zero
outside the domain: $z_k = y_k \cdot 1[k \in d]$ for a total, and the
corresponding residual for a mean (Särndal et al. 1992, section 10.3). Cutting
the sample into pieces first would treat the number of rows that fell in each
piece as fixed, which it is not.

## Which variance estimator, for which design

| Design | Estimator | `method` | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| simple, stratified, temporal, spatial, reservoir, multistage | Sen-Yates-Grundy with exact $\pi_{kl}$ | `"analytic"` | exact, unbiased |
| cluster | between-cluster form over cluster totals | `"analytic"` | exact, unbiased |
| cluster with `balanced = TRUE`, multistage with a take that depends on the clusters selected | two-stage formula at each cluster's take, weights conditional on the clusters selected | `"analytic"` | unbiased |
| weighted, `"poisson"` | $\sum (1-\pi_k) y_k^2 / \pi_k^2$ | `"analytic"` | exact, unbiased |
| weighted, `"systematic"` | Deville (1999) | `"deville"` | approximation |
| systematic | successive differences (Wolter 2007) | `"successive difference"` | approximation |
| systematic, `n_starts` of 2 or more | random groups (Wolter 2007) | `"analytic"` | exact, unbiased |
| stratified, `within = design_systematic()` | successive differences within strata | `"successive difference"` | approximation |
| spread | local means (Stevens and Olsen 2003) | `"local mean"` | approximation, conservative |
| certainty | whatever `rest` uses | as `rest` | as `rest` |
| any, on request or as fallback | jackknife, stratified where there are strata | `"jackknife"` | approximation |

### Sen-Yates-Grundy

For a fixed-size design with known joint probabilities,

$$\hat V_{\mathrm{SYG}} = \frac12 \sum_{k \ne l \in s}
\frac{\pi_k \pi_l - \pi_{kl}}{\pi_{kl}}
\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k} - \frac{y_l}{\pi_l}\right)^2$$

is unbiased whenever every $\pi_{kl} > 0$ (Sen 1953; Yates and Grundy 1953).
For stratified simple random sampling it reduces to the textbook
$\sum_h N_h^2 (1 - f_h) s_h^2 / n_h$, with $s_h^2$ the variance of $y$ among
the rows sampled in stratum $h$. Simple random, reservoir and spatial samples
are the case of a single stratum, and temporal intervals are strata. For
`design_multistage()` with the same take of $m$ rows from each of $a$ clusters
selected out of $A$, it reduces to the two-stage formula

$$\hat V = A^2 \left(1 - \frac{a}{A}\right) \frac{s_t^2}{a} +
\frac{A}{a} \sum_{i \in s} N_i^2 \left(1 - \frac{m}{N_i}\right)
\frac{s_i^2}{m},$$

with $s_t^2$ the variance of the estimated cluster totals $N_i \bar y_i$ and
$s_i^2$ the variance within cluster $i$. `drawn` computes these forms, which
take time and memory in proportion to the number of sampled rows. The sum over
pairs needs matrices with a row and a column per sampled row, more than a
gigabyte at 4,000 rows.

Under proportional allocation, an $n$ that does not divide by the number of
clusters, a cluster smaller than the take, or `design_cluster(balanced = TRUE)`,
the take $m_i$ from cluster $i$ depends on which clusters were selected. A
row's inclusion probability then averages over every selection; only the
balanced design has a closed form for it, and none of them has one for the
joint probabilities. `draw(weights = TRUE)` weights such a sample conditional
on the selection, $\pi_k = (a/A)\, m_i / N_i$, so the estimated total is $A/a$
times the sum of the estimated totals of the selected clusters, unbiased given
the selection and so over every selection. The formula above, with $m_i$ in
place of $m$, is unbiased for its variance. Given the selection, the estimated
cluster totals also vary by the variance within each cluster, so the first term
holds $(A/a)^2 (1 - a/A)$ times the within-cluster variances on average, and
with the second term that makes $(A/a)^2$ times them, the variance of the
estimate given the selection. What remains of the first term is the variance
between clusters.

The condition matters. **A stratum with one sampled row** has no pair inside it,
so it silently contributes nothing: with one row in every stratum the sum is
exactly zero. `drawn` declines in that case rather than report it:

```{r lonely}
set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(g = rep(1:10, each = 20), y = rnorm(200, rep(1:10, each = 20), 3))
one_each <- draw(pop, design_stratified("g", n = 10), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)
ht_total(one_each, "y")
```

### Cluster sampling

Taking whole clusters makes the number of *rows* random whenever clusters differ
in size, which violates the fixed-size assumption behind Sen-Yates-Grundy. The
cluster is the sampling unit, so the estimator is applied to cluster totals
$u_c = \sum_{k \in c} y_k / \pi_k$: $\hat V = (1 - a/A)\, a\, s_u^2$, the
simple-random form over $a$ of $A$ clusters.

### Poisson sampling

Rows are selected independently, so $\pi_{kl} = \pi_k \pi_l$ and the
Horvitz-Thompson variance collapses to $\sum_s (1 - \pi_k) y_k^2 / \pi_k^2$.

### Systematic PPS: Deville's approximation

`design_weighted(method = "systematic")` shuffles the frame and walks the
cumulative probabilities (Madow 1949; Hartley and Rao 1962). Its joint
probabilities have no closed form. Deville's estimator needs only the
first-order ones:

$$\hat V = \frac{1}{1 - \sum_s a_k^2} \sum_{k \in s} c_k
\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k} - \hat A\right)^2, \quad c_k = 1 - \pi_k,\;
a_k = \frac{c_k}{\sum_s c_l},\; \hat A = \sum_s a_k \frac{y_k}{\pi_k}.$$

Each row is weighted by its own $1 - \pi_k$, so rows taken with certainty drop
out, as they should. Matei and Tillé (2005) found it the most reliable of the
standard approximations for high-entropy designs. It equals
`sampling::varest()`.

### Systematic sampling: successive differences

A systematic sample has one random start. Most pairs of rows can never be drawn
together ($\pi_{kl} = 0$), so no design-unbiased variance estimator exists at
all. The successive-difference estimator compares each sampled row with its
neighbour in the order the design walked (Wolter 2007):

$$\hat V = (1 - f)\, \frac{n}{2(n-1)} \sum_{j=2}^{n}
\left(\frac{y_{(j)}}{\pi} - \frac{y_{(j-1)}}{\pi}\right)^2.$$

When the interval $k$ does not divide the $N$ rows the design walks, the sample
holds $\lfloor N/k \rfloor$ or $\lfloor N/k \rfloor + 1$ rows, and the total
moves with that count. Successive differences cannot see it, so
$\bar u^2 (r/k)(1 - r/k)$ is added, with $\bar u$ the mean of $y/\pi$ over the
sample and $r$ the remainder of $N/k$. Without the term a constant $y$ would
get a variance of 0.

Sorting the frame on something related to $y$ is what makes systematic sampling
efficient, and this estimator can see that where the simple-random formula
cannot:

```{r sdiff}
set.seed(12)
frame <- data.frame(x = runif(400, 0, 100))
frame$y <- frame$x + rnorm(400, 0, 20)
sorted <- design_systematic(interval = 10, order_by = "x")

# The truth, by enumerating all ten starts
starts <- vapply(1:10, function(st) {
  10 * sum(draw(frame, design_systematic(10, start = st, order_by = "x"))$y)
}, numeric(1))
true_var <- mean((starts - mean(starts))^2)

est <- vapply(1:200, function(i) {
  s <- draw(frame, sorted, seed = i, weights = TRUE)
  c(successive = ht_total(s, "y")$variance,
    as_if_srs  = 400^2 * 0.9 * var(s$y) / nrow(s))
}, numeric(2))
round(rowMeans(est) / true_var, 2)
```

Both are ratios to the true variance; the successive-difference figure is far
closer. Its limits are shared by every estimator from a single systematic
sample: a
frame that cycles with a period matching the interval, and a trend so smooth
that the random start is almost the only source of variation, both make it run
low.

### Several starts: random groups

`design_systematic(interval = k, n_starts = m)` draws $m$ different starts
from $1, \dots, mk$ and walks each at a step of $mk$. Every row keeps
$\pi_k = 1/k$, and two rows in different residue classes modulo $mk$ can now
be drawn together, with $\pi_{kl} = (m-1)/(k(mk-1))$. Each start gives a
replicate whose own total $\hat t_r$ estimates $t$, the sample's total is
their mean $\bar t$, and

$$\hat V = \left(1 - \frac1k\right) \frac{1}{m(m-1)}
\sum_{r=1}^{m} \left(\hat t_r - \bar t\right)^2$$

is the random group estimator (Wolter 2007), unbiased on $m - 1$ degrees of
freedom. It equals the Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator over the exact
$\pi_{kl}$, so `method` is `"analytic"`. The price is a step $m$ times as
long, so each replicate follows a sorted frame less closely, and few degrees
of freedom: with four starts a 95% interval uses $t_3$.

`design_stratified(within = design_systematic(order_by = "x"))` instead walks
each stratum from a start of its own, at a step of $N_h / n_h$ rows. The
variance is the sum of the strata's successive-difference approximations,
on the degrees of freedom of a stratified sample.

### Spatially balanced samples: local means

`design_spread()` selects by the local pivotal method (Grafström, Lundström and
Schelin 2012), which makes neighbours unlikely to be sampled together. That is
exactly the gain, and a simple-random variance would throw it away. The local
mean estimator compares each sampled row with the mean over its neighbourhood
$N_k$ — itself and its three nearest sampled neighbours:

$$\hat V = \sum_{k \in s} \frac{|N_k|}{|N_k| - 1}
\left(\frac{y_k}{\pi_k} - \frac{1}{|N_k|}\sum_{l \in N_k}
\frac{y_l}{\pi_l}\right)^2$$

(Stevens and Olsen 2003; Grafström and Schelin 2014). It errs conservative,
more so as the sampling fraction grows. Rows that a `size` column puts past
certainty are in every sample, so the sum leaves them out, as rows and as
neighbours.

### The jackknife

The delete-one-unit jackknife works from the sample alone. Units are clusters
where the design has them and rows otherwise, and where the design has strata
they are deleted *within* their stratum, with only that stratum reweighted —
the stratified or JKn jackknife (Wolter 2007, chapter 4). Deleting across strata
would count the differences between strata as sampling variance, which is what
stratifying removes. Each stratum carries its own finite population correction.
Units taken with certainty, whether past certainty on size, in a stratum taken
whole or in a census, are in every sample, so they are held fixed instead of
deleted and the correction counts only the other units.
For a stratified design the result equals the analytic figure exactly:

```{r jkn}
strat <- draw(pop, design_stratified("g", n = 40), seed = 2, weights = TRUE)
c(analytic  = ht_total(strat, "y", variance = "analytic")$se,
  jackknife = ht_total(strat, "y", variance = "jackknife")$se)
```

`variance = "auto"` uses the design's own estimator, and the jackknife only
when that declines — for instance a multistage sample with one row per cluster,
where the within-cluster variation cannot be measured and the delete-a-cluster
jackknife gives the standard ultimate-cluster approximation. It is refused for
systematic samples, whose primary sampling units are their starts rather than
their rows, and Poisson samples, whose exact variance it understates.

## Confidence intervals

Intervals use Student's $t$ on the design's degrees of freedom — primary
sampling units minus strata — rather than the normal distribution (Korn and
Graubard 1999). With hundreds of units the two agree; with a handful of
clusters the normal interval is badly short:

```{r coverage}
set.seed(5)
clus <- data.frame(cl = rep(1:24, each = 10))
clus$y <- rep(rnorm(24, 50, 20), each = 10) + rnorm(240, 0, 5)
truth <- sum(clus$y)

hits <- vapply(1:500, function(i) {
  r <- ht_total(draw(clus, design_cluster("cl", n_clusters = 4), seed = i,
                     weights = TRUE), "y")
  c(t = r$ci[1] <= truth && truth <= r$ci[2],
    normal = abs(r$total - truth) <= qnorm(0.975) * r$se)
}, logical(2))
rowMeans(hits)
```

Pass `df = Inf` for the normal interval.

Units taken with certainty count in neither number. They are in every sample
and carry no variance, so counting them would make the interval too narrow.
With eight certain units among ten, systematic PPS had 9 degrees of freedom
where the variance rests on two units, and the interval covered 79%. A sample
with no unit below certainty has a variance of 0 and `df = Inf`.

## How it was checked

Every estimator is checked in the package's tests against the empirical
sampling variance of its own estimator over many repeated draws, and every
inclusion and joint probability against the observed frequency. A condensed
version, run when this page was built — the ratio of the average estimated
variance to the actual variance of the estimates (1 is perfect), and the
coverage of the nominal 95% interval:

```{r check-all}
set.seed(7)
N <- 300
frame <- data.frame(
  site = rep(c("a", "b", "c"), times = c(150, 100, 50)),
  cl   = rep(paste0("c", 1:30), each = 10),
  x    = runif(N), yy = runif(N)
)
frame$size <- rgamma(N, 3, 0.2)
frame$y <- 2 * frame$size + 30 * frame$x + rep(rnorm(30, 0, 8), each = 10) +
  rnorm(N, 0, 6)
truth <- sum(frame$y)

designs <- list(
  simple        = design_simple(n = 40),
  stratified    = design_stratified("site", n = 40),
  cluster       = design_cluster("cl", n_clusters = 6),
  multistage    = design_multistage("cl", n_clusters = 8, n = 32),
  pps_poisson   = design_weighted("size", n = 40, method = "poisson"),
  pps_systematic = design_weighted("size", n = 40, method = "systematic"),
  spread        = design_spread(c("x", "yy"), n = 40, scale = FALSE)
)

check <- function(d, R = 400) {
  out <- vapply(seq_len(R), function(i) {
    r <- ht_total(draw(frame, d, seed = i, weights = TRUE), "y")
    c(r$total, r$variance, r$ci[1] <= truth && truth <= r$ci[2])
  }, numeric(3))
  c(variance_ratio = mean(out[2, ]) / var(out[1, ]),
    coverage = mean(out[3, ]))
}
round(t(vapply(designs, check, numeric(2))), 2)
```

With a few hundred replicates the ratios carry Monte Carlo error of several
percent; the test suite uses more.

## Agreement with `survey`

`as_svydesign()` expresses each design in `survey`'s own terms (Lumley 2004),
and the tests assert that the two packages agree to floating point on totals,
standard errors, domain estimates and degrees of freedom for every design
`survey` can represent exactly. Units taken with certainty go to `survey` as
one sampling unit per stratum, taken whole, so that neither package counts
them among the degrees of freedom. For systematic PPS, `survey` uses Brewer's
approximation and `drawn` uses Deville's. The degrees of freedom still agree,
and the standard errors of totals usually agree within 0.3%, but those of
means can differ by several percent when the sampling fraction is large.
`?as_svydesign` has the full table.

`survey::as.svrepdesign()` cannot build replicate weights from `survey`'s
own PPS and Poisson designs, and for a systematic sample it builds a
jackknife that ignores the order of the walk. `replicate_weights()` builds
them from the sample instead: the jackknife above for most designs, and
successive differences along the walk for a systematic sample, with no
pair joining the two ends of the walk. The standard error of a total is
then the one `ht_total()` gives:

```{r replicates, eval = requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)}
sys <- draw(frame, design_systematic(interval = 10, order_by = "size"),
            seed = 3, weights = TRUE)
rw <- replicate_weights(sys)
rep_des <- survey::svrepdesign(
  data = sys, repweights = rw, weights = ~.weight,
  type = attr(rw, "type"), scale = attr(rw, "scale"),
  rscales = attr(rw, "rscales"), combined.weights = TRUE
)
c(drawn = ht_total(sys, "y")$se,
  survey = as.numeric(survey::SE(survey::svytotal(~y, rep_des))))
```

Calibration is left to `survey` too. `frame_totals()` gives the population
totals `survey::calibrate()` takes, from the frame stored with the sample
and over the rows the design could reach, so the totals need not be built
by hand. Here `size` is known for every row of the frame and related to
`y`, and calibrating a simple random sample to its total narrows the
standard error:

```{r calibrate, eval = requireNamespace("survey", quietly = TRUE)}
srs <- draw(frame, design_simple(n = 40), seed = 3, weights = TRUE)
totals <- frame_totals(srs, ~size)
totals
cal <- survey::calibrate(as_svydesign(srs), ~size, population = totals)
c(horvitz_thompson = ht_total(srs, "y")$se,
  calibrated = as.numeric(survey::SE(survey::svytotal(~y, cal))))
```

With `table = TRUE`, `frame_totals()` gives the counts in each cell of its
variables instead, for `survey::postStratify()` and `survey::rake()`.
